sections.heading: The a element: content plus destination
sections.body: A link is an a element ('anchor') whose href attribute holds the destination URL: Example. The content between the tags — the link text — is what the visitor sees and clicks; the href is where activating it navigates. Browsers style links to be recognisable (blue and underlined by default), make them focusable with the keyboard, and let them activate with Enter as well as a click. Both halves are essential. An a element without href renders as plain text: not clickable, not focusable, announced as nothing special. And an href without meaningful link text is a destination nobody can identify. The a element is an inline element, so it lives naturally inside sentences and paragraphs — a few linked words mid-sentence is the web's native pattern, not a limitation to work around.
sections.code: The full reference lives at MDN Web Docs.

sections.heading: Absolute URLs: the complete address
sections.body:
An absolute URL is self-contained: scheme (https://), domain (developer.mozilla.org), and optionally a path to a specific page (/docs/Web/HTML). Because it carries every part of the address, it works identically no matter which page contains it — which makes it the required form for links leaving your site.

Always prefer the https:// scheme when linking out; linking to the insecure http:// version of a site that supports encryption sends visitors through an unnecessary redirect at best. You will sometimes see scheme-variants in the wild — mailto:someone@example.com opens the visitor's mail client, tel:+301234567 dials on phones — all still absolute URLs, just with different schemes.

The temptation to resist is using absolute URLs for your own pages. <a href="https://mysite.com/about.html"> works in production and silently breaks everywhere else — your local files, a staging server, a moved domain. Internal links have a better tool.
sections.code: HTML reference Email us

sections.heading: Relative URLs: addresses from here
sections.body:
A relative URL omits the scheme and domain and states only a path, which the browser resolves against the current page's location: on any page of your site, href="about.html" means 'the file about.html next to this page'. The same markup then works on your laptop's file:// copy, on staging, and in production, because the destination travels with the site.

Relative URLs can reach into folders (articles/first-post.html), climb out of them (../index.html) and anchor to the site root (/contact.html) — the full path grammar gets its own dedicated lesson next. For now, the rule of thumb: external links absolute, internal links relative.

One more relative form worth recognising: href="#section-id" jumps to the element with that id on the current page — the mechanism behind tables of contents and 'back to top' links. It combines with paths too: articles/guide.html#setup opens the page and scrolls to the section.
sections.code: About this site My first post Back to top

sections.heading: Link text: name the destination
sections.body:
Link text is read in three situations you must design for. In context, by sighted readers scanning for the highlighted phrases. Out of context, by screen-reader users who list all links on a page and jump between them — each link is announced by its text alone. And by search engines, which treat the text as a human-written description of the target page.

'Click here', 'here', 'read more' and bare URLs fail all three. The fix is to link the phrase that names the destination: instead of 'Click here to see the syllabus', write 'See the course syllabus' with 'course syllabus' as the link. The surrounding sentence usually gets shorter, not longer — the instruction to click was never information.

Two related quality rules: keep link text reasonably short (a phrase, not a paragraph), and never give two links with the same text different destinations on one page — 'Details' four times pointing four places is a maze for anyone navigating by links.
sections.code:
Click here for the syllabus.

See the course syllabus.

sections.heading: Linking images and larger blocks
sections.body:
Anything inside an a element becomes clickable, and the most common non-text content is an image: wrap an img in a link and the picture is the button. The site logo linking to the home page is the canonical example, a convention users expect on effectively every site.

A linked image's accessible name comes from the img's alt attribute, so the alt should describe the link's destination, not the artwork: alt="SkillStack home", not alt="Blue hexagon logo". An empty alt on a linked image creates a link with no name at all — one of the most common accessibility failures on the web.

Modern HTML also permits wrapping entire blocks — a card with a heading, image and teaser paragraph — in one a element, making the whole card clickable. It is legitimate and widely used; the trade-offs to know are that the link's announced name becomes everything inside it (keep card content concise) and that you cannot nest another link inside. What remains invalid is a link inside a link, and links inside buttons.

sections.heading: Link states: unvisited, visited, and friends
sections.body:
Browsers track which URLs you have visited and style links accordingly — the classic scheme is blue for unvisited links, purple for visited ones. The state lives in the browser's history, not in your markup: the same link renders differently for different visitors, helping them remember which paths they have already explored. On content-heavy sites like documentation or search results, that purple is genuinely useful wayfinding.

Two more states complete the set: active, the moment a link is being pressed (briefly red by default), and — though not a link-specific state — focus, the outline shown when a keyboard user tabs onto the link. CSS can restyle all of these (with :link, :visited, :active and :focus selectors, in that order), which you will meet in the CSS course.

The design lesson to carry from here: these states carry real information, so when styling links later, keep visited and unvisited distinguishable where history matters, and never remove the focus outline without replacing it — keyboard users navigate by it.

lessons.summary: Read and write every kind of path — same-folder, subfolder, parent with ../, and root-relative with / — plus the index.html convention and the file-naming rules that keep links working.
lessons.goal: Link the pages and images of a small multi-folder site using the correct path form for each relationship.
lessons.whyItMatters: Broken images and dead links are the most common beginner bugs, and virtually all of them are path mistakes — a file moved, a ../ miscounted, a space in a filename. Paths are also universal knowledge: the same grammar addresses files in CSS url() values, JavaScript imports, terminal commands and configuration files, so mastering it once pays off across every tool you will ever use. A site whose internal links are written correctly can move between your laptop, staging and production without a single edit.

lessons.prompt: my-site/ index.html contact.html images/logo.png articles/ first-post.html
lessons.explanation: Every relative path is read from the location of the file that contains it. From index.html at the top of the project, contact.html is a plain filename because the two files share a folder, and the logo and article need one folder step down — images/ and articles/ — before the filename. From first-post.html inside articles/, reaching index.html requires one step up, written ../. The path is not a property of the target file but of the journey from source to target, which is why the same destination gets different paths from different pages.
lessons.example:
A student builds a site where every image loads perfectly — until they reorganise pages into folders, and every picture breaks at once.

Nothing is wrong with the images: the pages moved, so every relative journey from page to image now starts somewhere else. Rewriting the paths relative to each page's new location (or switching shared assets to root-relative paths like /images/logo.png before deploying to a server) fixes the whole site. Understanding that paths describe journeys, not destinations, turns this from a mystery into a two-minute fix.

Add links to the contact page and the article, show the logo from the images folder, write the ../ link the article page would use to come home, and add one root-relative link. commonMistakes: Counting ../ steps wrong. Each ../ climbs exactly one folder; from articles/first-post.html one ../ reaches the site root, not two.
Spaces and capitals in file names. 'My Page.HTML' becomes %20-encoded in URLs and breaks on case-sensitive servers — use lowercase-with-hyphens.html.
Starting a path with / while testing from file://. Root-relative paths resolve to your disk's root locally; they only behave on a web server.
Writing paths that work by accident on Windows with backslashes. URLs always use forward slashes, on every operating system.
lessons.proTip: When an image or link breaks, open DevTools' Network tab and reload: the failed request shows the exact URL the browser assembled from your path — compare it with where the file actually lives and the miscounted step is usually obvious.

sections.heading: Path anatomy: journeys, not names
sections.body:
A path is a journey from one file to another, written as folder steps separated by forward slashes with the target filename at the end: articles/first-post.html means 'enter the articles folder, then open first-post.html'. The slash is always forward — URLs use / on every operating system, including Windows.

The defining fact about relative paths, worth reading twice: they are resolved from the location of the file that contains them. The same target has different paths from different starting points, and moving a file invalidates every relative path written inside it. When a link or image breaks, your first question is always 'where does this journey start?'

A project's folder tree is therefore something you must be able to picture. Sketch it, keep it shallow, and group by type or section — an images/ folder for pictures, an articles/ folder for posts — so that paths stay short and predictable.
sections.code:
my-site/
  index.html
  contact.html
  images/
    logo.png
  articles/
    first-post.html

sections.heading: Same folder and subfolders
sections.body:
The two simplest journeys cover most links on a small site. When source and target sit in the same folder, the path is just the filename: from index.html, href="contact.html" reaches its neighbour. No slash, no prefix — the browser looks right next to the current page.

To descend into a subfolder, name the folder, a slash, then the file: from index.html, the logo is src="images/logo.png" and the article is href="articles/first-post.html". Deeper nesting chains naturally — articles/2026/august/report.html — each slash one step down.

You may also see a leading ./ meaning 'the current folder': ./contact.html is identical to contact.html. Some developers and tools prefer the explicit form; in hand-written HTML the bare filename is the norm and this course uses it.
sections.code: Contact First post

sections.heading: Climbing out: the ../ parent step
sections.body:
The special segment ../ means 'the parent folder — one level up'. A page inside articles/ reaches the site's front page with href="../index.html": climb out of articles/, then open index.html. Steps chain: ../../ climbs two levels, and climbs combine with descents — from articles/first-post.html, the logo in images/ is ../images/logo.png (up out of articles, down into images).

Miscounted ../ steps are the classic path bug, and the reliable technique is to trace with a finger on the folder tree: start at the file containing the path, move up once per ../, then follow the named folders down. Every professional debugs paths exactly this way; nobody computes three levels of ../ in their head reliably.

If a path needs more than two ../ steps, treat it as a signal: either the folder structure is deeper than the site needs, or the next section's tool — root-relative paths — is the better fit.
sections.code: Home

sections.heading: Root-relative paths: anchored to the site root
sections.body:
A path that starts with / ignores the current page's location entirely and begins at the site root — the top of the domain: href="/contact.html" reaches the same file from every page on the site, however deeply nested. For shared elements like navigation menus that appear on every page, this is a huge simplification: one identical set of paths works everywhere, and pages can move between folders without their nav breaking.

The critical caveat: 'site root' is defined by a web server. When you open files directly from disk with file://, the leading / resolves to your drive's root — nowhere near your project — and every root-relative path breaks. So the rule of thumb: while learning with local files, use relative paths; once a site lives on a server (or a local development server), root-relative paths become available and are the standard choice for shared assets and navigation.

This also explains a pattern you will meet in real projects and templates: full sites tend to write /images/logo.png and /css/main.css, precisely so the references are location-independent.
sections.code: Home Contact

sections.heading: File naming: the rules that keep URLs clean
sections.body:
File and folder names become parts of URLs, and two naming habits prevent almost all name-related breakage. First, no spaces: a space is not legal in a URL and gets encoded as %20, producing addresses like my%20page.html that are ugly, error-prone and easily mangled when shared. Use hyphens where a space wants to be: my-page.html. (Hyphens are also preferred over underscores — they are the word separator search engines expect.)

Second, all lowercase, always. Your laptop's file system is probably case-insensitive, so About.html and about.html look interchangeable — but most web servers run on case-sensitive systems, where a link to about.html cannot find About.html. Sites that 'worked on my machine' and 404 in production are overwhelmingly casing bugs. A strict lowercase-with-hyphens policy makes the mistake impossible.

Keep extensions honest too: .html for pages, and the real extension of each image format. The name before the extension should say what the file is — first-post.html beats page2.html for every human and search engine that reads the URL.

sections.heading: index.html: the front-door convention
sections.body:
When a browser requests a folder rather than a file — https://example.com/ or https://example.com/articles/ — the web server looks inside that folder for a conventionally named default file and serves it. That name is index.html. It is why a homepage URL needs no visible filename: example.com quietly serves example.com/index.html.

The convention shapes how you structure and link sites. Name every folder's landing page index.html, and link to the folder for cleaner URLs: href="/articles/" reads better than href="/articles/index.html" and reaches the same document. Your site's front page is always index.html at the project root — build tools, hosting platforms and other developers all assume it.

With this, the path toolkit is complete: same-folder names, subfolder descents, ../ climbs, root-relative anchors, clean naming and index defaults. Every asset reference in the rest of this course — images, stylesheets, scripts — reuses exactly this grammar.
